extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate / graduate students of mechanics and applied mathematics (studying the calculus of variations)
extracted.subtask_description: Deriving the necessary conditions (and handling boundary terms) for a function y = φ(x) to make a given functional U a maximum or minimum, with attention to fixed vs free endpoints and continuum/virtual-displacement issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Total variation / extremum condition (DU = 0)
rubrics_metrics.description: The total change in U, called DU, consists of the differential (due to limits) and the variation (due to change in the form of the function); to obtain a maximum or minimum one sets DU = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for both contributions to DU — changes of the integration limits and changes in the function form — when forming the extremum condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate limit (boundary) contributions from interior variation
rubrics_metrics.description: After integration by parts the expression for DU contains (a) terms depending solely on the variation of the limits, (b) terms depending on changes in the form of the function at the limiting values, and (c) terms depending on the general change in the form of the function (interior integral).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect all terms except the interior (last line) under one designation (a1 − a0) and treat the parenthetical interior expression as P; the extremum condition then splits into boundary conditions and an integral condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boundary-term vanishing: a1 − a0 = 0
rubrics_metrics.description: The coefficients arising from the variation of the limits must satisfy a1 − a0 = 0 (equation (a) in the text).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These boundary/coefficient terms must vanish independently of the integral term, since the integral of an arbitrary function cannot be expressed solely by its limiting values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interior integral condition (Euler's equation / P = 0)
rubrics_metrics.description: The integral of P·δy over the domain must vanish for arbitrary δy; therefore the integrand P must be identically zero — this is the differential equation (Euler's equation) the extremal function must satisfy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because δy is arbitrary, the only way the integral can be zero in general is to make P = 0 throughout the domain; this yields the Euler–Lagrange differential equation (referred to as equation (3) in the text).

rubrics_metrics.name: Eliminate higher-derivative variation terms by successive integration by parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Variation produces terms containing δ(dy/dx), δ(d2y/dx2), ... which are dependent on one another; these are eliminated by repeated integration by parts using ∫u dv = u v − ∫v du.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply successive integrations by parts between the limits so that the final integral expression contains only δy under the integral sign, leaving separated boundary terms and an interior integrand P.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arbitrary constants determined by boundary conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: The differential equation (Euler's equation) generally contains several arbitrary constants; the values of these constants are determined solely by the conditions at the limits (the subsidiary/boundary conditions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solve the Euler equation to find the family of extremals (with arbitrary constants), then apply the appropriate boundary conditions (from a1 − a0 = 0 and endpoint specifications) to determine the constants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case: fixed endpoints (both x and y fixed)
rubrics_metrics.description: If both the limits X0, X1 and the endpoint values y0, y1 are given (fixed), then δx0 = δx1 = 0 and δy0 = δy1 = 0, so the boundary coefficients vanish and the coefficients of (dy/dx), d(dy/dx^2), ... independently vanish; constants are determined by the subsidiary conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In this case the interior Euler equation alone determines the functional form, and the given endpoint values determine the constants appearing in the general solution (example: shortest line → dy/dx = a constant, resulting in a straight line through given endpoints).

rubrics_metrics.name: Case: fixed x-limits but free endpoint y-values (natural boundary conditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the x-limits X0, X1 are specified but y0, y1 are indeterminate (free), then δx0 = δx1 = 0 while δy0 and δy1 are arbitrary; the boundary conditions imply certain coefficients (e.g., a) must vanish, leading to different classes of extremals (example: straight line y = b parallel to abscissa when a = 0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When endpoint y-values are free, the vanishing of boundary terms yields 'natural' boundary conditions (additional equations) which must be used together with the Euler equation to determine the extremal and constants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between actual increments and virtual displacements
rubrics_metrics.description: A distinction is made between increments of coordinates that actually take place in time (dx, dy, dz) and the possible displacements (virtual displacements) considered in principles like virtual velocities; virtual displacements are generally not variations unless the system is a continuum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only for continuum mechanical systems (strings, flexible surfaces, elastic bodies, liquids) may dx, δy, dz be regarded as indeterminate functions of coordinates and thus treated as variations in the calculus of variations framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notation caution (Lagrange vs Jellett)
rubrics_metrics.description: Jellett remarks that Lagrange's use of the symbol d in the first two terms V1 dx1 = V0 dx0 is illogical; the increments of the independent variables should be denoted by the usual symbols dx0, dx1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful and consistent in distinguishing different types of differentials/increments when forming boundary terms and applying variation calculus.
